sm: The chair opens the November Design Review Commission meeting, explaining that it is an informal subcommittee of the historic zoning commission that guides applicants toward a certificate of appropriateness. Applicant participation is voluntary, changes are the applicant's choice, and there is no public comment. Eight items are on the agenda. The first item, awnings and signage at 234 Public Square, is skipped because the applicant has not arrived, and the second item at 932 West Main Street is delayed because the architect was caught behind a bad car accident on Highway 96. The group moves to item three, a canopy at St. Philip's Catholic Church on Second Avenue South.

Staff explain that the church annex, built around 1985, is listed as contributing, and the proposed canopy would be twelve feet deep and twenty-seven feet wide with a pedimented design matching the annex portico. Guidelines discourage new canopies unless appropriate on secondary facades, and staff ask about the roof shape and scale. Commissioners note the annex is not attached to the historic church and support the canopy as marking an important entrance. They suggest showing it beside the wider bank facade for scale and adding a detailed section drawing. The chair then introduces item four, a rear addition at 418 Boyd Mill Avenue, presented by Jacob Lane.

The applicant describes a rear addition to a ranch-style house, with matching gridless windows, lower sloped roofs, a green porch, and skylights over the kitchen requested by the client. Staff say the 1956 house sits in the Boyd Mill Avenue historic district and the addition appears to align with the guidelines. They need more detail on materials, siding reveal, and the lanterns, and note that the skylights are not visible from the street. Commissioners praise the design, learn the addition is thirty-seven percent of the existing footprint, and note the district aims to preserve mid-century ranch homes. They suggest labeling the metal kitchen roof on the drawings. The group then returns to item two at 932 West Main Street.

The owner of 932 West Main Street says the house lacks a master suite and that a past addition was a mistake. He makes two requests: a site visit, and flexibility on an alteration that may not fit the guidelines. Using AI-generated images with the trees removed, he and builder Michael Lee argue the 1974 addition would better match the original house, with roof height raised only thirteen inches rather than five feet. Staff respond that the elevation would no longer be subordinate and conflicts with guidelines on preserving roof forms. They add that a 1950 Sanborn map and a 1974 photo show the rear feature is historic, even if later altered.

Commissioners discuss whether the rear addition replaced an open two-story sleeping porch. The applicant says the whole addition dates from 1974, that no old framing remains, and that the master bedroom ceiling would be too low without the extra thirteen inches. Holly says the proposal looks more historic than what exists, but a commissioner points out the lot is a corner and highly visible. Commissioners ask what is actually driving the height and whether the walls have been opened up. The applicant says only a small stretch of road gives a view and that he hopes for a site visit.

Commissioners say the new renderings are better, but landscaping is not considered and height is the guideline issue. The applicant says the thirteen inches is a deal breaker for the master suite. Angela is open to a site visit and appreciates the care taken. Mary has long disliked the addition, hopes it could come down about a foot, prefers a plain cornice to dental molding, and also supports a site visit. Another member is torn between improving the building and sticking to the guidelines, and asks the applicant to verify that thirteen inches matches the brick courses shown in the drawings.

Commissioners continue to wrestle with the roof height. One says the silhouette of the old porch roof is the only historic feature left, and that evidence of the 1970s rebuild inside the walls would be compelling. Others suggest the lower ceiling and step down could tell the story of the former porch, perhaps as a sunroom, and that improving the look need not depend on adding height. Staff note the bylaws allow a special meeting for a site visit and offer dates.

Staff offer site visit dates of December third, seventh, or tenth, all at four in the evening, and the group chooses Thursday, December third at four p.m. at 932 West Main Street. Commissioners discuss whether removing broken guidelines while breaking one more is a net gain, and the applicant explains that leaving the existing height would leave the master ceiling under eight feet after leveling floors. The site visit will be outside only. The group then returns to item one, awnings and signage at 234 Public Square, where Tanya Embry presents a revised arched awning rendering and argues two separate businesses entitle her to three signs each under the guidelines.

Ms. Embry shows other striped awnings downtown and explains that black and white is her brand, and that she wants more foot traffic toward her corner of the square. Staff say the awning fits the opening better but must truly fit the arch, ask whether high-contrast stripes are appropriate, and explain that the building counts as one ground-floor retail space with a recommended maximum of three signs, not six. Angela and others favor the awning, but signage count concerns them. A commissioner suggests using the plywood-filled transom for signs, and Ms. Embry says she was denied that years ago.

Staff explain that letters on the wood transom would count as a second wall sign, and zoning allows one wall sign per building facade. Replacing the plywood with glass would make it a window sign. Ms. Embry says glass would require interior work and cost tens of thousands of dollars. She reads guidelines allowing up to three signs per tenant space but not extra signs for additional entrances. Commissioners discuss spandrel glass and how multiple LLCs could be abused. She notes three signs are approved today, a wall sign, window signs, and a sandwich board.

Commissioners see some flexibility because the building is wide and hard to sign, and several prefer a glass transom that keeps the arch height visible over awnings. Moisture behind floating glass is raised as a concern. Staff say wood-backed signs would be wall signs barred by zoning, and the only route is a variance from the Board of Zoning Appeals, since guidelines cannot override zoning. Some commissioners find the awning rendering poor and argue the two businesses deserve separate signs, while staff remind them that uses and interiors are not reviewed.

Ms. Embry says the awnings would cost about twelve thousand dollars each with the arched top, and staff note new awnings now need stamped engineered plans. Commissioners are split. Some say the awning achieves her goal and does no harm, while others say it covers the arched openings and could invite copies. They suggest showing exact drawings and keeping a glass transom as a backup. Ms. Embry says she is asking for grace and has been trying to work within the feedback, and staff will send an email recap.

Commissioners want to see the exact awning shape and a section, since a flattened segmental arch creates a compound curve. They also want a rendering from a distance and less busy striping, similar to other downtown examples. Some say spandrel glass transoms with signage are common in other cities. Commissioners agree painted letters on the transom would be a good solution, but it needs a variance from the Board of Zoning Appeals. Staff say they will not need engineering calculations at this stage, only full drawings showing form and shape. The chair then calls item five.

Eric McGinnis of Common Design Works presents a preliminary concept for 408 Church Street, the former Generations Church, which has a new lease of about thirty-five to forty thousand square feet for co-working, events, and continuing Sunday church use. He proposes a twenty-by-forty foot covered patio with exposed wood and a shingled roof where a playground now sits. Staff say the 1954 parish building has 1990s additions and is non-contributing. They say the canopy appears too large and complementary design is needed. They also note the proposed wall signs exceed the nine-square-foot recommendation and painting brick is not supported. Holly suggests making it a porch or a separate building.

Mr. McGinnis explains the owner dislikes adding more of the orange 1990s brick, and asks whether any brick treatment other than paint has been accepted. Mary says she cannot support painting the brick, and that better windows, gutters, and landscaping would help more. Brian notes the neighboring Kennedy House and the church across the street are historic and that timber framing does not fit the architecture. Others call the timber heavy and clunky and suggest a lighter porch. The applicant says he is negotiating between the owner and tenant and will use the feedback.

Commissioners suggest a one-level, flat or shallow-pitched porch wrapping the recessed double-door entry on several sides, with slender metal columns, giving shade and tables with better control over height. They describe the elevation as a mismatch of windows, vents, parapets, and Gothic doors, so a light wraparound canopy might tie it together. The recess is about five feet deep. After thanking Mr. McGinnis, the chair announces a ten-minute break.

After the break, the chair opens item six, the Harpeth River Bridge at East Main Street and Franklin Road. Greg Gamble represents the applicant, joined by city engineer Paul Holson, who has been the go-between with the state transportation department. Two of the three options shown earlier have been dropped, leaving a brick-only option. They measured the existing pillar bases at about twelve inches but found that proportionately too tall, so they propose an eight-inch base that nods to the taller original.

The team explains a column is being poured in the field this week for staff to inspect, and an on-site meeting is set for December first at four p.m. They show two railing options: the state standard with about eight-foot post spacing, and a more detailed option with extra columns, pickets, and two top rails. Light poles sit about fifty feet apart on piers, set by state photometric standards. Staff say the all-concrete option is proposed with vertical members in Franklin Green. Commissioners find the lower option simple but the top one busy, suggest removing some intermediate pickets, and say the inset panels on the piers look too slender.

Commissioners ask about lowering the speed limit to remove the pedestrian wall, and Mr. Gamble says the state has taken a firm position to keep it, even though the speed limit is not required for it. Commissioners suggest overlaying the plan view, showing light locations, and making the panels beefier or combining them into longer horizontal panels to reduce busyness. They also want pier and picket lines to relate across the sidewalk, and wish for wall-washer lighting. The team will revise drawings and send a recommendation to the Board of Mayor and Aldermen.

Commissioners note that a black-and-white drawing makes the panels look busier than concrete will, and the finish will be natural, not anti-graffiti paint. The commission says it supports continued advocacy to remove the pedestrian wall. The speed limit is thirty, and aldermen have mentioned twenty-five as a possible way to drop the wall requirement. Mr. Gamble will email four options. Next is item seven, revisions to buildings one through three at 209 Liberty Pike. Richard Munger of Courtland, which owns and operates about seventy thousand apartment units, says the company closed on the property last month and wants to remove the top story from all three buildings, reducing units from 222 to 179.

Mr. Munger and Mr. Gamble walk through before-and-after drawings. Building one keeps its sunken resident courtyard, about three feet below the Liberty Pike sidewalk. Elevations change with new brick colors, some window changes needed for code, and limestone replacing some board and batten and Hardy material. The refinements are the final staff condition of approval, requiring a new certificate of appropriateness before the building permit. The same top-floor removal and window and material changes apply to buildings two and three, which face the interior courtyard and the factory parking lot.

The applicant also asks for feedback on covering two outdoor areas, a second-floor porch on building one and a two-story volume on building two, with shade structures for residents. Staff say the height reduction helps scale, but ask for floor-to-ceiling heights to be confirmed and window and door specs included. They note the covered corner would be highly visible from Liberty Pike. Commissioners welcome the height reduction, dislike recessed top floors, and praise the added stone. Questions about the sunken courtyard follow, and the applicants clarify the grade and steps.

The applicants explain there is a fifteen-foot fall down the site and an accessible route between buildings one and two. Commissioners support a pergola over the rooftop gathering area, preferring light, slender metal such as black-painted or aged Corten steel to answer the industrial factory context. They like the reduction in cement board and batten. The applicants say the hardscape in the permit set became complicated and they will simplify it back to what was approved, working with staff, and the signage package will be simpler. Commissioners find the earlier 3D perspectives helpful and say they have rarely seen an applicant ask to lower the height.

Item eight is new construction at 234 and 242 Fifth Avenue North, presented by Brandon. The building has been pushed back about nine and a half feet, now twenty-two feet from the property line at the south end, matching the Storehouse setback, and the large and light pieces have been flipped. Detailing was lightened with brickwork, cornice work, window heads, thinner canopy with turnbuckle supports, and raised parapets. Staff say the placement still does not align with the guidelines and ask for adjacent floor heights, total building height, widths, material samples, and a darker recessed brick. They note signage exceeds height limits and streetscape elements need restudy.

Staff add that, because the site is partly in the floodplain, outdoor furniture must be permanently affixed or removed daily. Commissioners say the building has come a long way. Angela, Bob, and Mary welcome the setback and facade, while Holly finds the color palette too new. One member says the setback protects views of Storehouse number nine, so he is comfortable even if it misses the metrics. He asks for mullions in the single-bay window, is not sold on the two-story brick portal, and notes the site straddles the historic district edge.

Commissioners say new buildings should set themselves apart as new, and the changes are good, though the rendering looks stark and the two-story frame needs the right brick and mortar. They find the front promenade interesting, noting built-in benches avoid masking the parking garage with plants. The applicant calls it the least resolved piece, needed to meet a five percent formal open space requirement, with benches raised for floodwater flow. He asks about approving the building now and returning later for the front, and staff say a conditional approval can bring the landscape back to the historic zoning commission. Staff announce a site visit on December first and one on December third, both at four p.m., and the meeting adjourns.
